transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Record: On
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Sara Kim (BrightPath Head of ML), Tom Nguyen (BrightPath Platform), Priya Desai (BrightPath Security), Evan Li (PM)

Summary: Quick demo of Redwood structured output / JSON mode and function/tool-calling. Showed Console flows, API examples, and Redwood Optimize suggestions for structured outputs + guardrails. Discussed security (VPC/KMS/SOC2), latency/cost tradeoffs, and pilot next steps.

Topics: Structured output (JSON mode), schema enforcement, function/tool calling, guardrails, Console demo (Routes & Optimize), pilot/benchmarking plan.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I see we have the BrightPath folks and Priya from security, thanks for making time. Quick agenda: 1) show JSON-mode/structured output and tool calling, 2) Console + Optimize notes, 3) Q&A and next steps.
[00:18] Sara: Yep sounds good, we are mainly interested in deterministic JSON outputs for downstream systems and safe tool calls into our internal APIs.
[00:27] Tom: Also want to under understand latency impact if we force strict schemas, and cost implications.
[00:35] Ava: Totally. Diego will lead the demo and I can jump in for pricing/contract stuff. Diego, over to you.
[00:41] Diego: Cool, thanks. So I'm in the Redwood Console - first tab is the API playground. I'm going to switch the model into JSON mode which enforces a schema. Quick note, JSON mode is available for hosted + dedicated and we also expose the same API for private.
[01:05] [Diego shares screen] Diego: Alright I'm pasting a sample prompt and a JSON schema — this schema describes a patient summary object with fields: patient_id, diagnosis_codes (array), priority, recommended_actions (array of objects with action_type and confidence).
[01:25] Priya: Sorry can you paste the schema in the chat? Our security team wants to validate fields before we send anything.
[01:31] Diego: Yep pasted — link: https://redwood.docs/json-mode-examples (placeholder).
[01:40] Speaker 1 (Evan): Quick question: if the model hallucinatess a field, does Redwood drop it?
[01:46] Diego: Good question. JSON mode does two things: 1) it biases generation toward the schema and 2) we run a lightweight post-processor validator that can either drop non-matching fields, coerce types when safe, or return an error depending on route config. You can set the route to strict mode to reject non-conforming outputs.
[02:10] Sara: And that post-processing happens server-side in Redwood? Is the raw LLM text stored anywhere?
[02:18] Diego: By default, hosted logs token-level outputs for debugging but we have controls: for Dedicated and Private you can disable retention; for Private you own logs. We also integrate KMS — you can have payloads encrypted at rest. Ava can follow up with SOC2 docs.
[02:35] Ava: Yup I'll send SOC 2 and our security pack.
[02:38] Tom: On latency — if we add strict validation and re-asks, how much extra latency might we see?
[02:45] Diego: Typically small: the validator runs in a few ms. The bigger cost is if you enforce re-asks (retry with more instructions) or run multiple evals. In our benchmarks we see structured enforcement add 10-30ms on top of token latency for short outputs; longer outputs dominated by generation time. But of course depends on model size and sequence length.
[03:10] Priya: For compliance we need audit logs for every function call and response, and ability to redact PII. Can Redwood provide that?
[03:18] Ava: Yes, audit logs per request are in Console; for Dedicated we can keep longer retention and for Private you control retention. Redaction tooling is also supported via our SDKs. I'll include docs.
[03:30] Diego: Ok moving on — function/tool calling. I'm going to demo binding a function called get_med_history(patient_id) — the model returns a JSON payload that includes an "action": "call_get_med_history" and a structured body we map to the function.
[03:52] [Diego runs demo] Diego: Here the model outputs a call object. Notice in the Console trace we show the function payload and the subsequent API invocation. We support sync and async tool patterns and verify signature/shape before executing.
[04:10] Sara: If the model requests a function that doesn't exist, do you block execution?
[04:14] Diego: Yes — there's a whitelist per route. You can also enable deny-by-default and only allow declared bindings.
[04:22] Evan: And is there RBAC on who can create or edit function bindings?
[04:26] Ava: Yes RBAC in Console — you can limit to admins. We'll share screenshots.
[04:30] Tom: Can Redwood call our internal HTTP APIs behind a VPC? We need zero egress.
[04:36] Diego: For Private deployments you can host the runtime inside your VPC and the function calls run inside that network. For Dedicated we offer VPC peering and private links; we can discuss specifics with infra.
[04:50] Priya: What about secrets? We need KMS/HSM integration for API keys.
[04:55] Diego: We support customer-managed keys and HSM integrations for Private, and for Dedicated we can integrate with cloud KMS.
[05:02] Sara: Ok can you show a schema that includes nested arrays? We have complicated outputs.
[05:07] Diego: Sure — here's an example with diagnosis_codes array and recommended_actions array of objects. I'll trigger a few example prompts.
[05:20] [First run] Model output: the model returns the structure cleanly.
[05:28] Speaker 2 (Tom): Looks pretty good, though I see the confidence numbers are floats with long precision — can you coerce formatting?
[05:34] Diego: Yes, post-processing can coerce types and format numbers. You can also attach a transform hook that runs small JS to normalize values.
[05:44] Ava: This is a good point — Diego, maybe show how Optimize suggests quantization/model choice for such schema-heavy workloads.
[05:51] Diego: Sure — switching to Redwood Optimize section. Optimize runs workload analysis on your prompt set and suggests batching/caching/quantization settings. For structured outputs it often recommends slightly larger context windows and disables extreme quantization to preserve deterministic outputs.
[06:12] Sara: Do we get concrete cost savings numbers?
[06:15] Diego: Yup Optimize provides estimated token-cost savings and latency impact per suggestion. You can export recommendations to a CSV — here's a sample: https://redwood.docs/optimize-sample (placeholder).
[06:25] Evan: How does caching interact with JSON mode? If we cache prefixes could that leak PII between tenants?
[06:32] Diego: Caching is per-route and can be per-customer; for multi-tenant hosted setup we isolate caches. For Private you can control cache persistence. There is also prefix-scoped KV cache.
[06:45] Sara: Perf question: if we enable continuous batching, will that increase latency variance? We need consistent tail latencies.
[06:51] Diego: Continuous batching can improve throughput but you can cap batch delay thresholds. For strict latency SLOs we recommend dedicated capacity or smaller batch windows and avoid large batching.
[07:05] [Diego runs a second example showing guarded fallback] Diego: Now I'll demo guardrails — I intentionally ask for a disallowed action and the route-level policy blocks it and returns an error code with an explanation.
[07:22] Priya: Nice — we need those error reasons in audit logs.
[07:25] Diego: Yes they surface in the trace and can be exported to your SIEM.
[07:30] Sara: We plan to pipe outputs straight into our EHR ingestion pipeline, so strict schema is non-negotiable. If model returns partial outputs how does Redwood handle partials?
[07:39] Diego: You can configure partials to be rejected, coerced, or accepted with warnings. For ingestion flows we recommend reject-and-fallback where we call a deterministic rule-based extractor as a fallback.
[07:52] Tom: On the API side, do you support streaming JSON mode? We need token-level streaming for UX.
[07:58] Diego: We do support streaming — with structured outputs streaming works but the validator runs incrementally and final validation happens at the end. There is a small complexity if you require strict final schema — we buffer until completion then validate.
[08:18] Ava: Quick interjection — pricing note: structured enforcement and function calling are included; cost depends on model class, tokens and routing. I'll follow up with a pricing sheet.
[08:28] [Screen: Console Routes view] Diego: Here is Route config — you can toggle json_strict: true, post_processor: drop_extra_fields, function_whitelist: [get_med_history, update_care_plan]. Also you can attach Optimize recommendations to a route.
[08:50] Evan: How do rollouts work? If we change route to strict do we canary?
[08:54] Diego: Yes, there's a canary rollout option per route; you can do A/B or % rollouts and automatic fallback to previous route if error rate spikes.
[09:05] Sara: Any rate limits when calling internal functions? We will likely have high QPS spikes.
[09:10] Diego: You can set per-route quotas and per-function throttles; Dedicated gives predictable throughput.
[09:18] Tom: For the pilot, we'd like a benchmark harness. Can you run Redwood on a set of 500 prompts and return per-token latency and schema compliance?
[09:25] Ava: Yes we do that often — Diego can produce a benchmark plan and run it during the pilot.
[09:30] Diego: I'll prepare a harness and share results.
[09:33] [Demo: Showing API logs] Diego: Example trace shows request id, model version, time to first token, final validation status, function call logs.
[09:45] Priya: About logs — can you redact PII before storage?
[09:49] Diego: You can configure pre-ingest redaction hooks or use our SDK to redact on the client side.
[09:58] Sara: Ok switching gears — can you show the SDK example that binds a function and calls the API?
[10:04] Diego: Sure — code snippet: client.call({model: 'rwd-3b', json_schema: schema, functions: [get_med_history], prompt: prompt}) and the response returns {output: {...}, calls: [{name:'get_med_history', args: {...}}]}.
[10:22] Speaker 1 (Tom): Does the client validate locally before sending to reduce cycles?
[10:26] Diego: There's client-side validation you can enable to catch obvious mismatches; server still enforces final validation.
[10:33] Ava: Quick note on models: for deterministic JSON we often recommend mid-sized sized models with temperature near 0 and explicit instructions — sometimes larger models help but at cost. Optimize can recommend a model/quantization profile.
[10:50] Sara: About quantization — will heavier quantization increase hallucination risk?
[10:55] Diego: Aggressive quantization can degrade determinism for complex structured outputs. Optimize will flag that.
[11:02] Evan: For the pilot could you suggest config for cost vs quality?
[11:06] Diego: Yes, I'll attach three profiles: conservative (high-quality), balanced, and cost-optimized.
[11:11] Priya: Security question — do you support single-tenant encryption keys per customer?
[11:16] Ava: Yes customer-managed keys per account for Dedicated/Private.
[11:19] Tom: Any compliance tension with streaming? We need to prove no data egress.
[11:23] Diego: For Private we run entirely in your network; for Dedicated we have VPC options and private routing to minimize egress.
[11:32] Sara: Ok can you demo a failure case? Like schema mismatch and fallback to rule-based extractor.
[11:37] Diego: Sure — feed noisy note, model returns missing diagnosis_codes; route config triggers fallback to our extractor which pulls codes using regex rules and attaches provenance.
[11:52] Ava: That provenance is important for your audit trail.
[11:55] Priya: Do you sign the function calls in audit logs? We need tamper evidence.
[12:00] Diego: We add request IDs and you can push logs to a signed storage; we also support append-only logs with cryptographic verification in Private setups.
[12:12] [Diego scrolls to Console: Optimize recommendations view] Diego: Optimize recommends disabling heavy quantization, increasing max tokens slightly, and enabling conservative post-processing for your workload. It shows estimated cost delta and expected schema compliance rate.
[12:35] Sara: How accurate are those compliance estimates?
[12:38] Diego: They are heuristic based on a sample of your prompts — usually within 5-10% of observed compliance. For pilot we compute ground truth.
[12:47] Evan: On rollouts — if we push a stricter route and errors spike, will Redwood auto rollback?
[12:51] Diego: Yes auto-fallback based on configurable error-rate or latency thresholds.
[12:57] Tom: Can we integrate with PagerDuty for alerts?
[13:00] Ava: Yes Alerting hooks and webhooks supported.
[13:05] [Long pause while Diego prepares a notebook]
[14:20] Diego: Ok back — here's a notebook we run locally for the pilot. It's in the repo I just shared: https://drive.redwood/demo-notebooks/brightpath-pilot (placeholder). The harness exercises 500 prompts, tracks schema compliance, TTF, TTF token, and function call accuracy.
[14:40] Sara: Perfect. Can you also include an example of a schema evolution — adding a new field without breaking older pipelines?
[14:47] Diego: Sure — we support schema versioning and migrations with route aliases. You can map old fields with transformers. I'll include an example.
[15:00] Priya: A couple of final questions from security: 1) encryption in flight and at rest (TLS and KMS) — yes?
[15:07] Ava: Yes TLS for all traffic, and KMS options as mentioned.
[15:10] Priya: 2) Do you have SOC2 and pen-test reports?
[15:13] Ava: Yes, will share SOC2 + pen-test summary.
[15:17] Priya: 3) Data residency — we need EU data residency for backups.
[15:21] Ava: We have region options and can store backups in EU for enterprise contracts.
[15:27] Tom: One ops question — how do we monitor per-route token spend?
[15:31] Diego: Console exposes per-route token and cost breakdown, and you can export to billing.
[15:36] Evan: Any gotchas for streaming with function calls?
[15:40] Diego: If you need mid-stream function calls we recommend the async pattern; streaming + sync function invocation is supported but final validation still needed.
[16:00] Ava: Ok let's do a quick recap and action items.
[16:05] Sara: Quick clarifying Q: when you say "post-processor can drop fields" — will it also include a reason in logs?
[16:11] Diego: Yes each action has a reason code in the trace.
[16:15] Ava: Recap — Diego will share sample schema, demo notebook, and benchmark plan; I'll send pricing and security docs; BrightPath will share prompts and success criteria. Plan to start pilot week of 2025-03-17.
[16:30] Tom: Thanks, that works.
[16:33] Sara: One more — what's the expected engineering lift to integrate function bindings? Our platform team is small.
[16:38] Diego: Minimal for basic bindings— a few endpoints and a small adapter. We'll provide SDKs and examples. For advanced workflows we can do a short integration sprint.
[16:50] Ava: I'll propose a Statement of Work after pilot scope is agreed.
[17:00] [Cross-talk about calendar availability]
[17:20] Priya: Thanks everyone, good demo. We'll review docs and get back.
[17:30] Ava: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the materials.
